newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Fiat sees 1997 group sales on rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fiat sees 1997 group sales on rise.

text.p: Italian industrial and carmaking giant Fiat said on Monday that its 1997 sales are expected to be around 90 trillion lire ($54 billion), while profits for the year will not be below the levels seen in 1996.

The group's chairman Cesare Romiti told the Turin-based daily La Stampa, "Forecasts for Fiat's 1997 turnover are for around 90 trillion lire," and added profits would not dip below 1996 levels when stripping out big capital gains made in 1996.

Analysts said that Fiat's sales line had been helped by Italy's new car incentive programme -- giving price discounts to new car buyers who trade in cars older than 10 years -- while there were signs operating profits were starting to improve.
Romiti's comments helped Fiat shares minimise losses and the stock ended with a loss of 0.69 percent at 5,433 lire while the Milan bourse's MIB30 index fell 1.6 percent,
Fiat saw 1996 sales rise four percent to 78 trillion lire, while in the first quarter of 1997 group sales rose 4.4 percent to 20.844 trillion lire.

Romiti added that for 1997, "I can forecast that we will eliminate debts, the financial position will be profit making and results will not be less than 1996 not counting the capital gains of last year."

Fiat showed a net consolidated profit in 1996 of 2.371 trillion lire from 2.147 trillion lire in 1995. In 1996, Fiat's profits gained from the partial flotation of its New Holland farm machinery arm and the sale of fund management group Prime to insurer Generali. Net debt at end-1996 was 2.2 trillion lire.
Romiti added in the interview that he saw no signs yet of an Italian economic upturn, and that a fall in Italian inflation was mainly due to the economy's weakness.

"The country still has a desperate need of growth and the economy does not seem to show signs of awakening," he said. Italian consumer price index (CPI) inflation has been slashed to an estimated 1.5 percent year-on-year in May from 4.3 percent a year ago.

The "record fall in prices is certainly due to the anti-inflationist policy of the government and the rigour of the Bank of Italy, but it cannot be denied that it is also linked to the weakness of the economy," Romiti said. ($1=1,665 lire)
